Οἱ στρατηγοὶ λέγουσιν ὅτι χειμὼν τὴν σωτηρίαν ἐκώλυσεν. φασὶ γὰρ προστάξαι ἄλλοις τὰ ναυάγια ἀνελέσθαι, αὐτοὶ δὲ πρὸς τοὺς πολεμίους πλεῖν. ἡ θάλαττα χαλεπὴ ἦν, καὶ οὐ ῥᾴδιον ἦν ποιεῖν τὰ προσταχθέντα. οἱ δὲ κατήγοροι οὐ ταὐτὰ λέγουσιν. ἕκαστος τοῖς πολίταις πειρᾶται τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γνώμην πιστὴν ποιεῖν.

paragraphs.greek: Ὁ ἀναγνώστης ἀκούει τοὺς μὲν λέγοντας τάδε, τοὺς δὲ ἄλλα. ὁ συγγραφεὺς δείκνυσι τὸν δῆμον ὀργιζόμενον καὶ τοὺς ῥήτορας διαφερομένους. οὐ ταὐτόν ἐστι τὸ ἀκούειν τοῦ λόγου καὶ τὸ εἰδέναι τὴν ἀλήθειαν. τίς οὖν τοὺς μάρτυρας ἐξετάζει; πόσος χρόνος δίδοται τῷ κατηγορουμένῳ; τὸ χωρὶς ἕκαστον κρίνειν ἔχει σημασίαν πρὸς τὸ δίκαιον.

Πρότασις γίγνεται περὶ πάντων τῶν στρατηγῶν μιᾷ ψήφῳ κρίνειν. τινὲς δὲ λέγουσιν ὅτι τοῦτο παρὰ τοὺς νόμους ἐστίν. οἱ πρυτάνεις πρῶτον οὐκ ἐθέλουσι τὴν ψῆφον διδόναι· ἔπειτα οἱ πολλοὶ φοβούμενοι πείθονται. Σωκράτης δὲ οὐ συναινέσειν φησίν. οὐ γὰρ ἄλλο τι ποιήσειν ἐθέλει ἢ κατὰ τὸν νόμον. τὸν λόγον τοῦτον ὁ Ξενοφῶν περὶ αὐτοῦ γράφει.

Οὐ μὴν ἡ τοῦ Σωκράτους ἀντίρρησις ἔσωσε τοὺς στρατηγούς. ὕστερον οἱ παρόντες ἓξ κατεκρίθησαν καὶ ἀπέθανον. ὁ δὲ Ξενοφῶν καὶ τὴν μεταμέλειαν τοῦ δήμου διηγεῖται. ἡμεῖς οὖν διακρίνωμεν τὴν ναυμαχίαν, τὴν κατηγορίαν καὶ τὴν κρίσιν. ὁ περὶ τῆς νίκης λόγος οὐ λύει πάντα τὰ περὶ τῶν ἀπολομένων· ἡ δὲ ὀργὴ οὐκ ἀντὶ τῆς ἀποδείξεως ἐστίν.

reading.translation:
After the naval battle near Arginusae the Athenians have victory, yet they do not simply rejoice. Many soldiers have perished, and anger arises over those not rescued. Relatives ask who is responsible. The generals come to the city and give an account. Victory does not remove the need to examine what has been done.

The generals say that a storm prevented the rescue. They say that they ordered others to recover the wrecks, while they themselves sailed toward the enemy. The sea was rough, and it was not easy to carry out the orders. The accusers do not say the same things. Each tries to make his own account credible to the citizens.

The reader hears some saying one thing and others something else. The writer shows the people becoming angry and the speakers disagreeing. Hearing an account is not the same as knowing the truth. Who therefore examines the witnesses? How much time is given to the accused? Trying each person separately has significance for justice.

A proposal is made to judge all the generals by a single vote. Some say that this is contrary to the laws. The presiding officials at first refuse to put the vote; then most give way out of fear. Socrates says that he will not agree. He is willing to act only according to law. Xenophon writes this account about him.

Socrates’ objection nevertheless did not save the generals. Later the six who were present were condemned and died. Xenophon also narrates the people’s regret. Let us therefore distinguish the battle, the accusation, and the judgment. An account of victory does not resolve everything concerning those who perished; anger is not a substitute for proof.

sections.title: 1. Infinitive reports and relative time
body: After verbs such as φημί and νομίζω, an assertion can be reported with an infinitive. A different expressed subject normally stands in the accusative: φησὶ τὸν ἄνδρα λέγειν. If the subject is the same as the reporting verb, it is often omitted and predicates may remain nominative: φησὶ δίκαιος εἶναι, “He says that he himself is just.”

In indirect statement, the infinitive’s stem can express time relative to the report: present λέγειν is simultaneous, aorist εἰπεῖν prior, future ἐρεῖν later, and perfect εἰρηκέναι a completed action with its resulting relevance. This reporting use differs from a complementary infinitive after “wish,” where aspect is central and the aorist does not simply mark past time.

sections.title: 2. Perception participles and finite reports
body: Verbs of perception or knowledge often take a supplementary participle agreeing with the person or thing perceived: ὁρῶ τὸν δῆμον ὀργιζόμενον, “I see the people becoming angry.” The participle is part of the complement, not merely an optional circumstantial addition. Its case agrees with the relevant noun.

Verbs of saying and knowing can also introduce finite clauses with ὅτι or ὡς. Do not substitute infinitives, participles, and finite clauses mechanically after every verb: the governing verb and intended meaning matter. Compare hearing a person speaking, hearing the report that something happened, and asserting that it happened.

sections.title: 3. φημί and negation
body: Learn present φημί, φῄς, φησί(ν), φαμέν, φατέ, φασί(ν), and imperfect ἔφην, ἔφησθα, ἔφη, ἔφαμεν, ἔφατε, ἔφασαν. Most present indicative forms are enclitic in their usual use; φῄς is accented. Position and neighboring accents can affect how enclitics are written in a sentence.

οὔ φημι can deny the embedded assertion: “I say that it is not so” or “I deny.” Check the scope of negation before translating word for word as “I do not say.” A negative inside a finite report normally stays with its own verb: λέγει ὅτι οὐκ ἦλθεν.

sections.title: 4. The articular infinitive
body: An article can turn an infinitive phrase into a noun-like unit: τὸ χωρὶς ἕκαστον κρίνειν, “trying each person separately.” The article is neuter singular; its case follows the phrase’s function. The infinitive itself does not acquire case endings.

An expressed subject of the infinitive is accusative. Other objects and adverbs remain inside the phrase. With prepositions, read the whole unit: πρὸ τοῦ τὴν βουλὴν κρῖναι, “before the council judges.” Here τὴν βουλήν is the infinitive’s subject, while τοῦ belongs to the entire infinitive phrase.

sections.title: 5. Relative antecedents, attraction, and prefixes
body: Normally a relative agrees with its antecedent in gender and number but takes case from its own clause. In attraction, a relative that would otherwise be accusative may adopt a genitive or dative antecedent’s case: τῶν ἀγαθῶν ὧν ἔχει, “of the good things which he has.” A relative can also have an understood antecedent: ὃ λέγει, “what he says.” Recover the clause’s function before parsing an attracted form.

Prepositional prefixes change spelling at boundaries. ἐκ becomes ἐξ before a vowel; συν- can become συμ- before a labial and συγ- before a velar; final vowels can elide, as ἀπό + ἄγω → ἀπάγω. A rough breathing can affect the final consonant, as κατά + ἵστημι → καθίστημι. Use these patterns to recover dictionary entries, not to invent a meaning from the prefix alone.

sections.title: Meet Xenophon’s Hellenica
body: Our selection moves back to 406 BCE, before Athens’ defeat, to the aftermath of Arginusae. Victory and a failed rescue produce competing reports and a dispute about procedure. This is historical narrative shaped through speakers and decisions. Identify where the generals explain themselves and where the narrator describes the assembly’s response; their claims are not interchangeable.

The seven books cover Greek affairs from 411 to 362 BCE, beginning where Thucydides’ unfinished history breaks off. They follow Athens’ defeat in the Peloponnesian War, oligarchy and democratic restoration, Spartan ascendancy, shifting alliances, and the rise of Thebes. The closing battle at Mantinea leaves uncertainty rather than a simple declaration that one city has permanently won.

Xenophon organizes political and military events through commanders, assemblies, negotiations, speeches, and judgments about conduct. His attention is selective, and his experience and sympathies shape the narrative. Ask what a speech tries to accomplish, whose actions receive explanation, and what a compressed transition leaves unclear. A historian’s ordering of events can be as significant as an explicit verdict.

Reading invitation: start with Book 2, chapter 3, on the Thirty, then follow chapter 4 through resistance and restoration. Compare the settlement with the later Eleusis episode instead of stopping at the hopeful return to Athens. Our module’s question has grown from control of appetite to restraint in civic life: what practices let former enemies inhabit one city? Read the complete work as a sequence of difficult choices, not a storehouse of uncomplicated moral examples.
The procedural dispute asks how a democratic assembly should exercise its power when anger is intense.

sections.title: Arginusae, 406 BCE
body: Athens won the naval battle at Arginusae, but failure to recover men from disabled ships and the sea became the subject of fierce accusation. The generals’ explanation involved a storm and delegated rescue duties. Xenophon reports competing claims and an emotionally charged political response. A military victory and responsibility for losses could be debated at the same time.

Do not confuse the council, the assembly, and an ordinary law court. The episode concerns an extraordinary collective proceeding against generals, not a template for every Athenian trial. The sequence of proposals and objections matters because procedure determines whose case can be heard separately.

sections.title: Socrates and the disputed vote
body: Xenophon reports resistance among the presiding officials to putting an unlawful proposal to a vote, followed by most giving way under pressure. Socrates refuses to act contrary to law. His objection is a concrete example of the tension between majority desire and procedural restraint.

The objection did not prevent the outcome. Six generals who returned were condemned and executed; Xenophon later describes regret and attempts to pursue those held responsible for misleading the people. Avoid a reassuring ending in which a principled refusal alone saves everyone.

sections.title: Build the sequence
body: Draw five boxes: victory, failed rescue and explanations, accusation, procedural dispute, outcome. Under each write who speaks and what the account establishes. Place Socrates’ refusal in the fourth box, not in place of the fifth. Explain why evaluating the rescue and evaluating the trial procedure are related but distinct tasks.

Translate one report in each form: infinitive, supplementary participle, and finite ὅτι clause. Then translate the final two paragraphs continuously. In your English, preserve the generals’ attribution and do not turn their explanation into an unqualified narrator’s fact.

questions.prompt: When was Arginusae?
Why separate council, assembly, and ordinary court?
questions.answer: The episode’s extraordinary procedure is not every Athenian trial.

questions.prompt: What did Socrates’ refusal accomplish in the narrated outcome?
questions.answer: It preserved his objection but did not prevent executions.

questions.prompt: Why distinguish rescue responsibility from trial procedure?
questions.answer: One question does not settle the other.
